subject: toucan
pitch: A keel-billed toucan showing off on a short mossy branch. A huge rainbow beak in lime green, sky blue and orange with a cherry-red tip, a glossy black body, a lemon-yellow bib, a ring of lime-green skin around each eye, bright blue feet and a scarlet patch under the tail. A single pink orchid blooms on the branch beside it.
reasoning:
I need to write a single TypeScript module using the SDK, keeping the code simple but functional with features I'm confident about. I'm thinking through realistic proportions for a keel-billed toucan model, with the beak around 0.19m and total body length near 0.5m including the beak.

The branch needs to rest on the ground since the whole model must stand at y=0, so I'll design it as a mossy log lying flat with the toucan perched on top, feet resting on the branch's upper surface. I'm sketching out the joint hierarchy next -- hips, chest, neck, head forming a spine chain -- with the bird's body tilted upright at roughly 45 degrees and the head angled forward and up, defining coordinates for the tail base, hips, and spine curve using a catmull path.

Setting up spine chain joints...

For the head, I'll parent it to the neck joint with an upward-forward aim. For the beak, I'm planning colored bands along a sweep—lime green at the base, transitioning through sky blue and orange to a cherry red tip—with a flattened box-like cross section to match a toucan's distinctive beak shape, and a separate darker lower mandible joint beneath the head.

For the head and face details, I'm using a sphere for the skull with a flattened, scaled sphere for the yellow chest bib, plus small torus shapes placed near the eyes to form lime-green eye rings, oriented to match the head's local positioning.

I'll simplify: just set eyes facing forward with dir [0,0,1] and axis "z", since exact precision isn't critical here—it just needs to run and look reasonable. Now moving on to the wings, which should look like glossy black folded membranes.

For the wings, I'll construct them as a flat extruded outline lying in the YZ plane along the body's flank, with the outline running backward and upward from an attachment point near the shoulder, giving a folded-wing silhouette roughly 0.2m long and 0.07m wide.

I'm working out the cross product confirming that the thickness direction comes out along X, which means both wings stay symmetric without needing mirrored directions — just mirrored X positions for left/right.

Now I'm planning the tail as a swept chain extending back and down from the hips, with a scarlet patch painted on the undertail coverts.

I'm sketching a sweep-radius function to taper the tail flat, then setting up the leg chains from the hip joints down to foot targets on top of a branch, working out the branch's position and radius so the bird's feet land correctly on its surface.

Now I'm rescaling the body's vertical proportions so the toucan perches properly — hips, chest, neck, head, and beak heights — and sizing the two-segment leg lengths so hip-to-foot distances work out with bends at the knee, then building the leg chain with named joints parented to the hips.

For the feet, I'm sketching three toes as small rods extending forward from each foot point, colored bright blue, with thin radii to keep them delicate looking.

Now I'm positioning the leg joints relative to the hips, mirroring left and right at x=±0.05, then working out the spine as a catmull curve running from the rump back point forward through the chest up to the neck and head, keeping the toucan's body horizontal with a slight tilt.

I'm defining the body as a swept chain along this spine, using a radius function that bulges in the middle for the chest and tapers toward the rump and neck ends.

Now I'm placing the head: a sphere attached at the end of the neck joint, working out the aim direction so the head points up and forward from the body.

I realize I should use the joint's own local coordinate system rather than raw model-space coordinates, so I'll position parts with `head.local(...)` instead of fixed offsets. Then I'm shaping the beak as a rigid sweep attached to the head bone, curving from a point near the face forward and downward with a tapering cross-section and colored bands along its length.

I'm adding a jaw joint beneath the head so the lower mandible can hinge independently, with its own bezier sweep running roughly parallel to the upper beak but slightly shorter and shallower.

For the eyes, I'm placing a small lime torus ring around a dark eye sphere to mimic the toucan's distinctive bare skin patch, keeping the proportions subtle against the black head.

Working out the exact eye position on the head sphere's surface, I'm computing lateral, forward, and vertical offsets so the eye sits just outside the head geometry rather than sinking into it, then figuring out the outward-facing direction vector accounting for how local-right maps to world-left in this coordinate frame.

For the direction parameter I'm settling on using model-space values directly since that's what the part function expects, aligning the ring with the Z axis. I'm now sketching the yellow bib geometry—placing a flattened sphere at the chest front and checking its scaled dimensions against the body's surface radius so it doesn't clip through.

For coloring, I'm keeping the body black with fixed roughness, then adding a scarlet patch under the tail by specifying a sector range with partial taper values. For the tail itself I'm setting up a short bone chain with two spans anchored to the hips joint, placing the first joint near the rump.

Now I'm sweeping the tail tube with a tapering radius function and applying the same red sector patch near its base. For the branch, I'm laying out a polyline running along the X axis with slight height and depth variation, then sweeping a tube along it with bark coloring, keeping the radius and center height matched so the flat-bottomed cross-section rests flush on the ground.

I'm figuring out how to make the branch look mossy by either painting a mottled green texture pattern across the bark surface or scattering small flattened sphere "moss" blobs across the top of the sweep using a surface scatter helper.

Now I'm planning an orchid next to the branch: a thin sweep for the stem rising from the branch's surface, with the flower built from petal shapes and a lip around a central point at the top.

Defining petal outline points...

Now I'm working out the flower geometry: a bigger magenta lip petal in front, yellow column sphere at center, with five petals arranged radially at 72° intervals around a center point. I'm debating whether petal orientation vectors should stand vertically like fins or tilt orthogonally to look more natural, leaning toward computing an orthogonal "up" vector relative to each radial direction for a more realistic tilted petal shape.

Simplifying: 5 pink petals arranged radially around the center, plus a small deep-pink lip sphere beneath. I'm defining each petal's outline as a rounded pointed shape extruded along the radial and tangent directions with slight thickness and bevel, then moving on to sweep the stem geometry.

Stem curve runs from the base near the orchid up to the flower center, colored moss with a thin radius, positioned beside the bird so it doesn't collide with the beak. I'm skipping extra leaves and buds to keep things lean, maybe adding one leaf at most, and now I'm settling on a color palette—glossy black body, lemon yellow bib, lime and sky blue accents, orange, cherry red, and a lime-green eye ring—keeping the total distinct flat colors within the 64-cell budget.

Rounding out the palette with bright blue feet, scarlet, moss greens for the branch, bark brown, two pink tones for the orchid, and a pale eye color. For the branch I'm defining a paint function that blends mottled moss coloring on the upper surface with plain bark coloring below, checking the surface normal's y-component to decide which texture applies, and confirming that paint functions can return another paint (like a mottle pattern) rather than just a flat color.

I'm setting the branch sweep to a constant 0.042 radius colored with the bark paint, confirming rounded end caps are fine since the branch tips sit away from the bird's body. I'm reasoning that unattached scenery like the branch and flower stem will default to riding the nearest joint (likely the hips) since they have no explicit bone, which is fine since they don't need posing. Finally I'm checking the toucan's feet placement against the branch's curved top surface, making sure the toes sit just above the branch line at the correct height and depth.

Working out the wing geometry now—placing it against the body surface near the hips, with an outline that folds back along the spine, keeping it black to match the rest of the figure. Then I'm adding eye detail: a small torus ring in skin tone around the eye socket, plus a tiny pupil sphere positioned slightly forward.

Setting up the builder imports and confirming paint/mottle functions come from the single SDK module, then defining the metadata and starting the spine chain as a catmull curve from hips through back, chest, and neck joints.

I'm placing the head joint at the end of the neck, adding a sphere part for the skull geometry, and now constructing the toucan's beak as a cubic bezier curve extending forward from the head.

Still writing beak geometry...

Adding eye rings and pupils...

Now I'm placing a yellow bib at the throat, sized and positioned so it sits proud of the chest surface just under the beak, then starting the body sweep with a radius that varies along the spine, tapering near the rump.

Next I'm setting up the tail as a chain of two bones following a curve from the hips outward and down, then sweeping it with a tapering radius and a scarlet sector marking for color detail. Finally I'm starting the leg setup, defining hip attachment points on each side of the body.

For each leg I'm using the limb helper with a hip and foot position and a single bend direction pointing backward to approximate a bird's knee joint, though I'm double-checking whether the bends argument needs to be wrapped as a nested array when there's only one inner joint.

Then I'm setting up the three-point chain for each leg with named hip/knee/ankle joints, and working out the toe geometry—three small rods fanning out from the foot point to toe tips, positioned so they rest just above the branch surface.

I'll give the toucan zygodactyl feet four toe rods, two forward and two back, colored to match the feet. Then I'm sketching the wings as extruded outlines in black positioned along the chest, checking that the thickness axis and bevel settings keep them properly aligned on each side of the body.

For the branch, I'm building a catmull-rom curve through several points to shape it, then checking the math so its lowest point barely touches the floor without sinking too far below y=0. I realize keeping all the branch points at the same radius and height would make the bottom flush with the ground plane, so I'm adjusting the curve points to use a consistent y-value throughout.

Now I'm defining the bark paint as a conditional between moss and bark based on normal direction, and setting up a mottled moss texture with some randomness to its pattern. For attaching moss, I'm scattering clumps across the branch's surface with a minimum distance between them and a filter condition to control placement.

For the orchid flower, I'm working out the stem path with a catmull-rom curve going up from the branch, then building the petal shapes using extruded outlines with vector math to position each petal radially around the flower's center. I need to make sure petal outline arrays with "sharp" corner markers get typed correctly as OutlinePoint tuples rather than plain strings.

I'm distinguishing the larger deep-pink lip petal from the other four petals, positioning it at a different angle with its own outline shape, and adding a small yellow sphere for the flower's column at the center. I'm deciding to skip adding separate leaves to keep the scope manageable.

I'm double-checking proportions throughout -- leg lengths relative to hip-to-foot distances, wing placement against the body's radius at that height, the eye ring torus size relative to the head, and beak shaping with color bands transitioning to a red tip. I'm confirming the various builder methods (rod, part, stick, extrude, sweep) take color either positionally or through their options object, and that paint functions returning either a color or a Paint object work correctly. With all this verified, I'm ready to write out the complete piece of code along with its final export.
